paras: The manhunt for Hanson Willis was the March 1888 pursuit through Jackson County, West Virginia, of a shantyboat dweller accused of shooting his father-in-law, George W. Carter, near Pomeroy, Ohio. Willis was reported to have killed one of his pursuers, a young man named Thornton, and dispatches said fifty to a hundred men would kill him on sight. One dispatch called the pursuers a "lynching squad," but they never caught him; Wheeling police arrested him in April, and he was indicted in Meigs County, Ohio, and sentenced to twenty years in prison.

Willis, his wife and at times her father lived in a shantyboat moored at points along both shores of the Ohio River. After Grover Cleveland's election as president he painted the name "Hanson Grover Cleveland Willis" on the boat beside the outline of a revolver and a warning, given as "Beware of me" or "Beware of me and my gun."

On an evening in mid-March, after the two men had been drinking and quarrelling, Willis was accused of firing six shots into Carter and killing him. Willis's wife went to the authorities and also accused her husband of killing a couple named Jennings at Point Pleasant and sinking their bodies in the river.

According to the Mason City account, "The sheriff and posse at once sought the boat," and the posse grew to fifty men as it followed his trail. Parkersburg dispatches said a first party of ten under McMillen Thornton, "a young business man," overtook Willis near Hereford. By these accounts Willis fired first, killed Thornton and wounded two others before escaping.

Reports of the renewed hunt stressed the intent to kill: a Parkersburg special said fifty men "will pursue him to death or capture," and another version said they "will kill Willis on sight." The Mason City correspondent put the party at "fully 100 men" and wrote that "No mercy will be shown him."

The pursuers did not find him; on March 27 he was seen drifting down the Ohio in a skiff, and "no one attempted to arrest him." Early on April 4, tipped off by the crew of the steamer Ben Hur, Wheeling officers John Shorts and Richard Wilkie disarmed and arrested him as he slept on deck.

When the officers took Willis to Pomeroy on April 5, crowds met the train at every station and a "tremendous crowd" lined the river bank there. The Meigs County grand jury indicted him for first-degree murder in Carter's death. In September he pleaded guilty at Pomeroy and was sentenced to twenty years in the Columbus penitentiary, on a plea the Wheeling Register gave as manslaughter and a Pomeroy correspondent as murder in the second degree. No report of an inquest or charge for Thornton's death appears in the coverage.

The story came from white West Virginia papers, chiefly in Wheeling, and was carried by wire from New York to Montana. Headlines played on his crimes and his adopted name, among them "Killed Four Men," "A Namesake of President Cleveland Pursued by Lynchers" and "After a Desperado."

Lynching language appeared only twice: the Charleston special called the pursuers a "lynching squad" and "Lynchers," and a Wheeling wire in the New York Sun said after the capture that "His chances for being lynched are considered good." Elsewhere the pursuers were a posse, a "band of prominent residents," or, in one capture wire, "the officers." That fall a Pomeroy narrative in the Atlanta Constitution and the St. Paul Daily Globe said his record had "seldom been paralleled outside of the wild west" and blamed his escape from the gallows on the county's wish to avoid the cost of a trial.

The Charleston special said the man killed was a detective named Thaxton, shot near "Mud Rock" or "Murdock" on the morning of March 20, while the Parkersburg, Mason City, Wheeling and Pomeroy accounts named McMillen Thornton, a young civilian, killed near Hereford.

Carter's killing is dated from March 14 to March 16 and placed at Racine, Letart, near Ripley Landing or near Pomeroy. The Omaha Bee and the Pomeroy narrative said Willis escaped unhurt, while he showed the Wheeling officers a wound he blamed on the posse.

reader.title: Manhunt for Hanson Willis
bases: An armed posse and bands of citizens hunted Willis for a murder, he killed one pursuer, and he was later arrested by police and imprisoned; no one was killed by the pursuers (A5, A6, A12, A18).
Willis was not killed; he was arrested by Wheeling police and sentenced in court (A12, A18), though the pursuers, fifty to a hundred strong, vowed to kill him (A4, A5, A8).
Independent Charleston, Parkersburg, Mason City and Wheeling reports agree on the pursuit and the killing of a pursuer (A2, A4, A5, A12).

accounts.gist: Detective Thaxton overtook Willis near Mud Rock/Murdock and was shot dead; a 'lynching squad' or 'Lynchers' were pursuing him.

accounts.label: Parkersburg dispatches
accounts.gist: A band of ten under McMillen Thornton overtook Willis near Hereford; Willis fired first, killed Thornton and wounded two; fifty men then took up the hunt vowing to kill or capture him.

accounts.label: Mason City correspondent
accounts.gist: The sheriff and posse sought Willis after his wife informed; the posse, grown to fifty and then 100, was ambushed and Thornton killed; 'No mercy will be shown him.'

accounts.label: Willis's own claim
accounts.gist: He killed in self-defense and was wounded by one of the posse.

accounts.label: Pomeroy retrospective
accounts.gist: An armed posse from Pomeroy, reinforced by Jackson County citizens, split into squads; one was surprised after midnight, Thornton was killed and Willis escaped unhurt.

framing.detail: Wheeling papers reported the hunt, the arrest and the sentence as crime news ('After a Desperado', 'A Four-Fold Murderer Captured'), stating the pursuers' intent to kill without comment.
Distant papers ran the Parkersburg and Wheeling wires under 'A Desperate Criminal', 'Hunting a Desperado', 'A Desperate Outlaw Captured'.
The Charleston special headlined 'A Lynching Squad After Him' and 'Pursued by Lynchers' with no criticism of the pursuers.
